opus-5.5.text:
I think the Bayesian paradigm is one of the most useful lenses we have, but I'd be careful about treating it as the whole explanation.

What it gets right is striking. If you look at how people generalize from very few examples, show a child three pictures of a dalmatian and call each one a "fep," and they'll quickly narrow in on what "fep" means. They don't need thousands of labeled examples. The Bayesian story explains that nicely: you have a space of hypotheses, a prior over them, and a likelihood that captures how well each hypothesis explains the data. Things like the size principle fall out naturally. If every example happens to be a dalmatian, it would be a suspicious coincidence if the word meant "animal," so you favor the narrower hypothesis. That's a deep insight, and work by people like Josh Tenenbaum and Tom Griffiths has shown that human judgments track these predictions surprisingly well.

Where I think it gets more interesting, and where I've spent a lot of my own thinking, is in the question of what the hypothesis space actually is. Bayes' rule is just bookkeeping; it tells you how to update beliefs once you've specified the hypotheses and the prior. All the real action is in those representations. Humans seem to reason over structured, compositional, almost program-like hypotheses: causal models, rules, simulations of the world. That's why I'm drawn to probabilistic programming, because it lets you write down rich generative models as programs and then treat inference as reasoning about which program could have produced what you observed.

There are also real tensions. Exact Bayesian inference is computationally intractable for anything interesting, so whatever humans are doing has to be some kind of approximation, and the specific approximations matter. Sampling-based accounts, for instance, can explain some of the ways people deviate from ideal behavior. And there's the question of where the hypotheses come from in the first place. People don't just weigh existing hypotheses; they invent new concepts, they ask questions, they run experiments. That active, constructive side of learning, the way a scientist or a child actually goes and intervenes on the world, isn't fully captured by passively conditioning on data.

So my view is that Bayesian inference is a good computational-level account of the logic of learning from evidence. But to really explain human learning, you need to pair it with a theory of rich representations, of resource-bounded inference, and of how agents actively seek out information and build new models. That combination is where I think the exciting work is.

r001.rationale: The response says Bayes' rule specifies how beliefs update once hypotheses and priors are set, while leaving the inference process and its implementation unresolved; it notes that the approximations humans use matter.

r002.rationale: It states that exact Bayesian inference is computationally intractable for interesting problems and that human inference must therefore be approximate.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, I'd say I have a kind of complicated relationship with the Bayesian paradigm. On one hand, I think it's probably the best formal account we have of what it means to learn from a small number of examples. If you show a child one or two instances of some new object and they can generalize from that, the question is, what's filling the gap? And the Bayesian answer is: prior knowledge. You come in with a structured hypothesis space, you have beliefs over it, and the data just shifts those beliefs. The reason you can learn from one example is that you've already done most of the work before you saw it. And I think that basic picture is right. Work from Josh Tenenbaum and others, the Bayesian program learning stuff, showed pretty convincingly that if you get the hypothesis space right, you can reproduce a lot of the qualitative patterns of human generalization, like how people pick the "right" level of abstraction, or why they infer rules rather than just interpolating.

But I think there are at least two places where I get uncomfortable treating it as the explanation. The first is that the paradigm is almost too flexible. Bayesian inference tells you how to update given a prior and a likelihood, but it says nothing about where those come from. And in practice, all of the interesting content lives in the choice of hypothesis space. So when a Bayesian model matches human behavior, you have to ask whether that's because humans are doing Bayesian updating, or because the modeler was clever about picking a representation. The inference part is almost the boring part. The hard problem, which is where the representations come from and how they're acquired, is largely outside the scope of what Bayes gives you.

The second thing is computational. Exact Bayesian inference is intractable for anything resembling a realistic hypothesis space, so you end up saying humans are doing some approximation, sampling or amortized inference or whatever. And that's fine as a research program, but once you say "approximately Bayesian," you've opened the door to a huge range of mechanisms, and a lot of the normative force of the framework gets diluted. A lot of the systematic deviations people show from Bayesian predictions might just be telling us about the algorithm rather than the ideal.

So where I land is that I think of Bayesian inference less as a theory of how humans learn and more as a specification of the problem they're solving. It's a very good way of stating what the right answer would be. The actual explanation of how the mind does it has to involve the structure of the hypotheses themselves, and I think program-like representations are a big part of that, plus some story about how you search over or construct those programs under resource constraints. The Bayesian view is the right lens for asking the question, but I don't think it's where the answer is.

r001.rationale: The response says Bayesian inference specifies how to update beliefs but leaves the mechanisms open, citing possible sampling or amortized inference and a broad range of mechanisms.

r002.rationale: It says exact Bayesian inference is intractable for realistic hypothesis spaces and that humans therefore use some approximation, such as sampling or amortized inference.

astra-6.text:
I think the Bayesian paradigm is useful, but it leaves an important question open. It gives you a way to update your beliefs given some evidence, assuming you already have a space of hypotheses and a model of how those hypotheses generate observations. But where does that space of hypotheses come from?

If you look at how people learn from examples, often they're doing more than adjusting their confidence in possibilities they've already considered. They're coming up with new explanations, or changing the representation of the problem. You can try to account for that within a Bayesian framework, but simply saying that learning is Bayesian doesn't yet explain how that happens.

So I'd distinguish Bayesian inference as a formal account of how beliefs should change from a mechanistic account of how humans actually learn. It's a useful language for describing parts of learning, but I don't think it gives you the whole explanation by itself.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes formal Bayesian updating from a mechanistic account of learning, but its specific open question is where the hypothesis space comes from—not how belief updating itself is implemented.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that people perform approximate rather than exact Bayesian inference.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the Bayesian paradigm gives us a useful account of what it means to learn from examples: you have some hypotheses about how the world works, and you update your beliefs as you see evidence. But a lot of the explanatory work is in specifying those hypotheses and the prior. What kinds of things can you represent, and why do you consider some explanations more plausible than others?

If you show someone a single example of a new concept, they can often generalize quite far. A Bayesian model can capture that, but only if it already has a sufficiently rich structure. So saying that humans are Bayesian doesn’t, by itself, explain that ability. We also need to understand where the structure comes from and how people actually carry out the inference.

I’d distinguish Bayesian inference as a normative framework—how you should update beliefs under certain assumptions—from a claim about the mechanism in someone’s head. The first can be useful without the second being literally true.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes Bayesian inference as a normative framework from the actual mechanism in someone’s head, explicitly leaving open how people carry out inference.

r002.rationale: It questions whether Bayesian inference is literally the mechanism, but does not say humans likely use approximate rather than exact Bayesian inference.
